newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. opens world debate amid doubts, gloom.
newsitem.headline: U.N. opens world debate amid doubts, gloom.

text.p: The General Assembly opened a three-week debate in a gloomy mood on Monday with U.N. finances in dire straits, its role uncertain and no sign of agreement on who should lead it into the 21st century.

"A stalemate persists, an uncomfortable stalemate that leads to a feeling of ... insecurity about the future of the United Nations," Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Palmeira Lampreia told the 185-nation General Assembly.
By tradition, Brazil is the first country to speak at the general debate of a new U.N. assembly session.

"In the wake of momentous changes in the international scene, the United Nations has embarked upon a new phase in its history without the means and the effectiveness to act as the highest political forum of mankind," he said.

World leaders called for political and financial reforms of the organisation at last year's celebrations to mark the U.N.'s 50th anniversary. Various committees and working groups were set up amid much fanfare, but one year later the United Nations is still owed nearly $3 billion in unpaid dues, more than half by the United States.

To the annoyance of many others, Washington has blocked the appointment of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali for the customary second five-year term. The United States says a more vigorous reformer is needed at the helm.

Discussions on many other reforms, including the issue of which countries should become new permanent members of the powerful U.N. Security Council, have become bogged down in disagreements and regional rivalries.

Most countries agree on the need for reforms and on the risks to the United Nations if it does not go some way to restoring the brief "golden age" of true cooperation that it enjoyed immediately after the end of the Cold War.

But there is no real agreement about how this should be achieved, and the United States is in the middle of an election in which the United Nations is regularly vilified by conservative Republicans as an enemy of U.S. interests.
The former Soviet republic of Georgia, Argentina, the Marshall Islands, Andorra and others laid out their different views on reform in the debate's first session on Monday.

"The 50th anniversary of the United Nations understandably raised the expectations of the international community ... We cannot say with the same confidence that the 50th anniversary has ushered in a renewed commitment to the U.N. and its future," Brazil's Lampreia told the assembly.

There are currently five permanent Security Council members who each have the power of veto -- the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain. Germany and Japan are prime candidates to join them, but there is little agreement on who should have a permanent seat among developing countries.

The financial crisis has led Boutros-Ghali and others to warn that the United Nations faces bankruptcy. But, after the failure of U.N. peacekeeping in Bosnia and Somalia, many countries are now wary of using the institution in conflict resolution -- one factor that could reduce U.N. bills.

One of the few real achievements of the 51st U.N. General Assembly will be the signing of a global treaty banning nuclear tests. The United States, Russia and other nuclear powers are due to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) on Tuesday, followed by other nations. But India's objections to the treaty and its refusal to sign could mean the agreement never enters into force.
